summary: Venamax is registered as alpha-lipoic acid, gamma-linolenic acid, vitamins, selenium and zinc. The FDA record does not itemize the vitamins or their amounts.
evidence: No clinical trials of Venamax itself were identified on PubMed.

Alpha-lipoic acid in kidney disease: in the PATH trial, 353 hemodialysis patients randomized to mixed tocopherols plus alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg/day or placebo for 6 months showed no effect on CRP, IL-6, oxidative-stress markers or erythropoietin response, with similar mortality and hospitalization (Himmelfarb 2014). A pilot RCT in CKD stages 3 to 4 also found no change in these markers (Ramos 2011).
No trials of gamma-linolenic acid for kidney outcomes were identified.
cautions: Ask for the full vitamin and mineral content: multivitamin blends may contain vitamin A or high-dose vitamin C, which patients with advanced CKD or on dialysis are usually told to limit. (Reviewer: confirm wording and add source.)
Alpha-lipoic acid may add to glucose lowering in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas; monitor glucose. (Reviewer: confirm and add source.)
Registered as a food supplement with no approved therapeutic claims; content and dose are not verified like a drug.
bottom_line: The best kidney trial of its main antioxidant ingredient (PATH) was negative. No basis to recommend it for kidney protection; check the vitamin content before a patient with advanced CKD takes it.

sources.citation: Himmelfarb, J., Ikizler, T. A., Ellis, C., Wu, P., Shintani, A., Dalal, S., Kaplan, M., Chonchol, M., & Hakim, R. M. (2014). Provision of antioxidant therapy in hemodialysis (PATH): A randomized clinical trial. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 25(3), 623–633.
